archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (pass-rush defense, broken run game)
archetype.definition: A roughly league-average team by efficiency and point differential whose 1-4 start comes from three one-score losses, poor special teams and penalties more than from how it actually plays.

report.headline: A .500-caliber team wearing a 1-4 record; Jacksonville is a real test.
report.take:
Houston has scored 110 and allowed 112. That is the season in one line. A team that is plus-three in turnovers, 14th in net EPA and 14th on both sides of the ball should not be 1-4. The gap shows up in a -1.91 wins over expected, 31st in the league. The Texans are 0-3 in one-score games, losing by five to Buffalo, two at Indianapolis and four to Dallas. Only the 20-6 loss to Cincinnati was a clean beating. These were coin-flip games, and Houston lost the coin flips with hidden yardage: special teams are 26th in EPA per game, and the team averages 8.4 penalties (24th), with three games of 83+ penalty yards.

The identity has flipped from last year. The 2025 team that went 12-5 won with the league's second-best defense and a 22nd-ranked offense. This year the offense is the steadier side, while the defense has slid to 14th. The offense is entirely Stroud's arm. The run game is the worst in football by yards per carry (3.03) and 31st in success rate, and that is with a 19th-ranked yards-before-contact figure. The line isn't the whole problem, but it isn't helping. The passing has heated up: after negative pass EPA in Weeks 2 and 3, Stroud posted +15.2 against Dallas and +10.5 at Tennessee.

The defense is a split personality. Play to play it is excellent: 4th in success rate allowed, 18 sacks (2nd), a 9% sack rate and a top-10 run defense. Then it gives up the big one. It is 26th in explosive pass rate and 26th in deep EPA allowed, and opposing WR1s are scoring 6.5 PPR points over their norm, 30th. That is a vertical-coverage problem, and it got worse when starting safety Jalen Pitre (92% of snaps) hurt his shoulder. The context helps a little. The 36 and 34 points came against the league's No. 1 and No. 4 offenses, and Indianapolis and Tennessee managed 22 combined.

The direction is up, but the hole matters. Eleven of the 12 remaining opponents have a worse net profile than Jacksonville, and a positive turnover margin with neutral efficiency usually produces a winning record over time. Still, Jacksonville is three games clear in the division. Houston's realistic path is the wild card, and it probably needs something like 8-4 the rest of the way.

strengths.title: A pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: Houston turns pressure into sacks at an elite rate. A middling 21.4% pressure rate (13th) has still produced the league's 3rd-best sack rate. Combined with a 4th-ranked success rate allowed, the down-to-down defense is legitimately good. Converting pressure to sacks this efficiently tends to cool a bit, but the hit rate (8th) says the rush is winning, not getting lucky.

strengths.title: Stroud's passing has caught fire
strengths.body: After a -9.7 pass EPA dud against Cincinnati, Stroud has produced +15.2 and +10.5 in his last two games. Pass EPA sits mid-pack (15th) for the season with the trend pointing up. Collins has drawn 25 targets in three games, the best per-game rate on the team, so a full-strength receiver room lifts this further. Because the run game contributes nothing, nearly all of the offense's value is coming through the air.

strengths.title: Underlying profile is .500 or better
strengths.body: Net EPA is 14th and the point differential is essentially even. The turnover margin is positive, so this isn't a team giving games away with interceptions. A 0-3 mark in one-score games and -1.91 wins over expected are the classic markers of a record that should catch up to the play.

concerns.title: A run game that doesn't function
concerns.body: At 3.03 yards per carry (32nd) with a 31st-ranked success rate, the offense has no ground leverage. Last season's offense was 22nd, so this isn't a total departure from history. Lead back David Montgomery is doubtful with a groin injury and right tackle Braden Smith is on IR, so it is more likely to get worse than better. That leaves Stroud facing predictable passing downs against good fronts.

concerns.title: Explosive passes over the top
concerns.body: The defense wins snaps and then gives up chunks: 26th in explosive pass rate and 26th in deep EPA, with opposing WR1s 6.5 PPR points above their norm. This is a real flaw rather than a fluke, since it showed up against Buffalo and Dallas. Losing Pitre makes it harder to fix.

concerns.title: Self-inflicted hidden yardage
concerns.body: Special teams (-2.54 EPA a game, 26th) and 8.4 penalties a game (24th) are exactly the margins that lost three one-score games. Penalties are a discipline issue a staff can tighten. Special teams are harder to fix midseason.

trend.note: The first three weeks were a 0-3 slide with a flat passing game. Weeks 4 and 5 brought the two best passing performances of the year and a 26-3 rout, though Tennessee's 31st-ranked offense flatters that defensive line.

nextGame.headline: Stroud must win deep against a top-three defense, without Montgomery
nextGame.body:
Jacksonville is the worst possible opponent for Houston's shape. The Jaguars' run defense ranks 3rd in EPA, which erases a Texans ground game that is already last in yards per carry and likely without Montgomery. Their short-pass defense is the best in the league, so the quick game won't bail Stroud out either. The opening is vertical: Jacksonville is 23rd in deep EPA allowed and has been badly hurt by WR2s and WR3s (30th and 32nd in PPR over average). That puts Houston's secondary targets on the spot more than Schultz, since Jacksonville has held TE1s 3.7 points under their norm. Once in close, Houston faces a defense allowing touchdowns on only a third of red-zone trips (2nd).

Availability cuts both ways. Houston likely loses Pitre (92% snaps) from a secondary that already leaks deep balls, plus Montgomery. Jacksonville is without safety Eric Murray (out), has right tackle Anton Harrison (92% snaps) questionable with a knee, and has corner Montaric Brown questionable. If Harrison sits, Houston's 3rd-ranked sack rate gets a line that is already 28th in QB hit rate allowed. The early forecast calls for 14 mph wind with gusts near 28, five days out. If it holds, it would cut into both teams' deep passing and the total, but it is too early to lean on.

keyMatchups.title: Houston pass rush vs. Jaguars' tackles
keyMatchups.body: Jacksonville's pressure rate allowed is good (8th), but its QB hit rate allowed is 28th, and Harrison's knee could open the right side. Houston's sacks are its most reliable way to stall a 7th-ranked passing offense. A couple of drive-killing sacks is how the Texans keep this low-scoring.

keyMatchups.title: Stroud deep vs. a soft back end
keyMatchups.body: With the run and the short game both shut off, Houston's offense lives or dies on intermediate and deep throws. Jacksonville's deep defense is its weak spot, and Murray's absence thins it further. Wind, if it materializes, is the threat to this plan.

keyMatchups.title: Houston's run game vs. JAX front
keyMatchups.body: Houston averages 3.03 yards a carry, and Jacksonville's run defense is 3rd in EPA and holds lead backs to the stingiest EPA in the league. Expect Woody Marks to find little. That makes Houston one-dimensional on early downs, which plays into Jacksonville's coverage.

nextGame.watch: Whether Houston's third and fourth receivers win downfield against Jacksonville's depleted secondary, because the run and short game won't be there.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the record to start matching the play. The schedule after Jacksonville is forgiving: Tennessee and the Chargers are both winless with bottom-two offenses, and Indianapolis, Washington and Philadelphia all rank in the bottom half on at least one side. Houston's even point differential, positive turnover margin and 0-3 one-score luck point to something near a .550 team from here, which lands around eight or nine wins. Catching Jacksonville from three back is unlikely, so the wild card is the real target.

What holds up: the pass rush, the down-to-down defense and Stroud's improving efficiency. What should regress in Houston's favor: the one-score record. What won't fix itself: the run game, especially without Montgomery and Smith. Big plays allowed will also keep giving up points to good offenses like Baltimore and Jacksonville in Week 15. The special-teams deficit is the quiet drag that could keep them on the wrong side of close games.
swingFactors: Close-game luck turning (0-3 in one-score games)
Deep-pass coverage holding up against good offenses

bets.reason: Jacksonville allows 14 points a game with the 2nd-best red-zone defense, and Houston's offense has no run game to sustain drives against a top-three rush defense. Houston's own defense ranks 4th in success rate allowed. Three of Houston's five games went under, and a possible gusty forecast is a small extra nudge.

The net EPA gap (3rd vs 14th) and Jacksonville's point differential (+10.6 a game vs -0.4) are larger than a home-field 3 implies. Houston's special teams and penalty problems also tend to show up on the road. Harrison's knee and Houston's pass rush are the risk, so this is only a modest edge.

confidence.note: Five-game sample; injuries to Pitre, Montgomery and Smith change the profile going forward.
